title: The Goal
blurb: A plant manager has three months to save his factory. A business novel about finding the one thing that holds a whole system back.

characters.name: Alex Rogo
characters.bio: 38, an engineer with an MBA, now running a factory in the town where he grew up. Works hard, sleeps little, and is starting to suspect the rulebook is wrong.

characters.name: Bill Peach
characters.bio: Alex’s old mentor, the man who sent him back to get his MBA. Now the division is losing money, and Peach’s own job is on the line.

characters.name: Bob Donovan
characters.bio: Six-foot-four, nine years running production. If something can be done, it’s done by the next time you ask.

characters.name: Julie Rogo
characters.bio: Followed Alex’s career to a town where she has no friends. She sees less of him every week.

characters.name: Jonah
characters.bio: Alex studied his mathematical models years ago. Now he studies how organizations really work, and he answers questions with questions.

characters.name: Lou
characters.bio: Two years from retirement. Mild-mannered until someone tries to fool him with numbers.

characters.name: Stacey Potazenik
characters.bio: Tall, brisk and direct. Fights over-production every month and gets blamed for the inventory anyway.

characters.name: Dave Rogo
characters.bio: Packed his dad’s gear the night before and dragged him out of bed for the troop’s overnight hike.

characters.name: Herbie
characters.bio: The slowest walker in the troop, carrying a pack that clanks like a junkyard. The others tease him; he keeps trying to keep up.

characters.name: Andy
characters.bio: First in line in the matchstick game, and the fastest walker in the troop.

characters.name: Evan
characters.bio: Last in line in the matchstick game, and first in line for washing dishes.

characters.name: Ralph Nakamura
characters.bio: Runs the plant’s computers. Quiet, careful, and usually ignored, until his numbers start answering real questions.

characters.name: Sharon Rogo
characters.bio: Second grader with straight A’s, who waits up by the window for her father.

characters.name: Johnny Jons
characters.bio: Sells for the division and catches the blame when orders are late. Loves a good bet.

characters.name: Hilton Smyth
characters.bio: Always promoting his latest productivity program. His indicators look great; his bottom line does not.

characters.name: Alex’s mother
characters.bio: Runs on ziti and worry. Will call the chairman of the board herself if anyone gives her son trouble.

characters.name: Bucky Burnside
characters.bio: Big, white-haired and hard to please. His company stopped buying from the division after too many late deliveries.

chapters.title: 90 Days
chapters.hook: Your boss is parked in your spot. Before your first coffee, your factory has 90 days to live.
recap: The Bearington plant is losing money and every order is late.
Peach’s deadline: three months, or the plant closes.
On paper everything looks fine. Nothing works.

posts.head: Your boss is parked in your spot.
posts.sub: Before your first coffee, your factory will have 90 days to live.

posts.label: Meet Alex Rogo · Plant manager · 38
posts.text: Alex gets in early every day to work before the phones start ringing. Not today. Four people rush him at the door: a supervisor, a union steward, a furious machinist and a foreman, all shouting at once. Behind them, nobody is working.

posts.label: Customer order

route.note: Still waiting its turn at an n/c machine

posts.text: Bill Peach, the division VP, arrived an hour earlier hunting this one late order. Every part was ready except one. Peach told the machinist to scrap a 90-minute setup for another ‘urgent’ job and run his part instead. The machinist refused. Peach threatened to fire him.
posts.foot: In this plant every order is urgent. So none of them ship on time.

posts.label: Alex’s office · Peach is sitting in Alex’s chair

msgs.text: Your plant is losing money, and it’s dragging the whole division down.
After the layoffs and the 20% cut you ordered, we’re lucky anything ships.
Look at your efficiencies. You have enough people. Use them.
Bill, I need time.
You have three months. Turn this plant around, or I recommend we close it.

posts.head: Then the key machine breaks.
posts.text: Tony, the master machinist Peach yelled at, quits. Before he goes, he sets up the job he was told to run but leaves two adjusting nuts loose. The NCX-10, the plant’s most expensive machine and the only one of its kind, breaks down mid-run.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Order 41427 has to ship tonight. You’re Alex. What do you do?

options.text: Put every available worker on this one order. Forget the usual rules.
options.feedback: Same call as Bob Donovan.

options.text: Stick to the schedule and protect the efficiency numbers.
options.feedback: The rulebook agrees with you. But nothing in the normal schedule gets 41427 out tonight.

options.text: Call Peach and ask for one more day.
options.feedback: Peach already promised the customer it ships today. That call would not go well.

posts.reveal: Bob Donovan, the production manager, pulled people from every department, ran overtime against policy and had parts carried by hand, one at a time. Just after 11 PM, the truck pulled away from the dock.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.take: Rushing one order through cost a machinist, a repair bill, overtime and every other order.
posts.label: Shipped just after 11 PM
posts.text: Over burgers and beer, Bob says he wishes they could move that fast every day. Alex says it would wreck their efficiency numbers. Keep this conversation in mind.

posts.label: Home · 6:30 PM
posts.text: Julie wants to go out to dinner. He has ten minutes. When he mentions the plant might close, she perks up: has he asked where they’d move next? She never wanted to live in his hometown. Driving back, he passes a dead factory with weeds in the lot. Two thousand jobs, gone. In three months that could be his plant.

posts.label: Alone in the corner office · late

items.text: Good people, a workable union contract
A market: competitors’ products are selling

posts.text: He has everything a factory needs. Yet every order is late, the floor is buried in half-finished parts, and the plant loses money. Something basic is wrong, and he can’t see what.

Tomorrow at 8 AM sharp, Peach has summoned his plant managers to headquarters. Nobody is told why. And in Alex’s jacket pocket is a cigar he was handed two weeks ago at an airport gate. Alex doesn’t smoke.

chapters.title: Five Minutes at O’Hare
chapters.hook: Five minutes in an airport. One question. Everything he believed about running a factory, wrong.
recap: The robots made one department look efficient. The plant earned nothing more.
Busy is not the same as productive.
Jonah’s question: what is the goal?

posts.head: Five minutes. One question. He couldn’t answer it.
posts.sub: It turned out to be the only question that mattered.

posts.label: UniCo HQ · 15th floor · 7:50 AM
posts.text: In the parking garage, a colleague pulls Alex aside. The rumor: unless results improve by year end, the whole division gets sold, and Peach goes with it. Suddenly Peach’s rage makes sense. Upstairs the slides roll: first-quarter sales down 22%. Alex reaches for a pen to take notes. He pulls out a cigar instead.

posts.label: Flashback · two weeks earlier
posts.text: Alex is between flights, on his way to speak on a panel about robots saving American factories. In a crowded airline lounge he spots a man in a sweater and a yarmulke, reading, cigar in hand. It’s Jonah, the physicist whose mathematical models Alex studied as a student.

msgs.text: My plant has robots. One department got 36% more productive!
So your plant makes 36% more money now?
Well, no. It was just one department.
Did you ship even one more product a day? Did your costs or your inventory go down?
…I’d have to check. Probably not.
Then the robots didn’t make you more productive.

posts.label: Jonah’s diagnosis
posts.h: He’s never seen the plant. He describes it anyway.

items.text: Machines run nonstop to keep efficiency above 90%

posts.text: Alex is stunned. How does he know? Jonah says the people reporting the numbers are honest. The measurements themselves are what mislead him.

posts.take: Productive means moving closer to the goal. Busy is not the same thing.
posts.myth: If every machine and every worker is busy, the factory is productive.
posts.truth: Productive means moving the company closer to its goal. Keeping everyone busy can move it further away.

posts.label: Jonah asks you
posts.q: What is the goal of a manufacturing company?

options.text: Produce products as efficiently as possible
options.feedback: That was Alex’s first answer. Jonah said: wrong.

options.text: Gain power
options.feedback: Alex tried this too. Jonah said not bad, but you don’t get power just by making things.

options.text: Win market share
options.feedback: Alex’s last guess. Jonah only asked, ‘Is it?’

options.text: Something else
options.feedback: Interesting. Hold that thought.

posts.reveal: Jonah won’t tell him. He says Alex can work it out himself. The answer arrives in Chapter 3, and your guess is saved.
posts.hint: Pick your answer. We’ll keep it for Chapter 3.

posts.label: Concourse · final boarding
posts.text: They race through the terminal, through security, past gate after gate, Jonah firing questions the whole way. What does being productive mean? Productive toward what? At the aircraft door, with the flight attendant glaring, he still won’t give the answer. He hands Alex a cigar, steps on board, and is gone.

Back in Peach’s meeting, twenty managers argue about productivity targets. Nobody has asked what the goal is. At the ten o’clock break, Alex packs his briefcase, walks to the elevator, and leaves his boss’s meeting.

chapters.title: The Goal
chapters.hook: He walked out of his boss’s meeting with a pizza and a six-pack. By the last beer, he’d found the answer.
recap: The goal of a business is to make money.
Measure it with net profit, ROI and cash flow, all rising together.
Unsolved: how does work on the floor connect to those numbers?

posts.kicker: A hill above the plant, 1 PM
posts.head: He skipped his boss’s meeting for a pizza, a six-pack and a hillside.
posts.sub: By the last beer, he had the answer headquarters never asked for.

posts.label: Looking down at the plant
posts.h: A gray box with no windows
posts.text: Down there sits a gray steel box. About 400 people are working inside. Trucks back up to one side carrying materials. Trucks leave the other side carrying products. He’s supposed to manage all of it. So what is it actually for?

items.why: Purchasing got great prices on a 32-month supply of copper wire. It sits in warehouses.
The plant has laid off hundreds already. Paying wages isn’t why it was built.
Rolls-Royce made superb products and nearly went bankrupt.
The VW Beetle was good and cheap to build. VW still stopped making it.
If tech were the goal, R&D would run companies. It always sits off to the side.
Millions in finished goods sit unsold in his warehouses. And you can win market share while losing money.

posts.take: Everything else is a means. Making money is the goal.
posts.label: The answer
posts.head: The goal is to make money.
posts.sub: Quality, technology, efficiency, good people, market share: each one helps a company make money. None of them is the goal.

posts.label: Back at the plant · 4:30 PM
posts.text: Alex catches three workers sharing a newspaper. He tells their supervisor to find them something to do. Minutes later they’re moving parts from one side of the aisle to the other. Then it hits him. They’re working now. Is any of it making the company money?

msgs.text: Say you’re rewriting the textbooks. What’s the minimum you’d need to know if we’re making money?
Net profit. How much we made, in dollars.
But $10 million is great on one million invested, and lousy on a billion. So you need return on investment too.
And a profitable company can still go under if it runs out of cash. So, cash flow.
So all three have to go up.
Two years from retirement, and now this. Okay, Al. I’ll help.

posts.take: Net profit, ROI and cash flow must all rise together.
posts.label: The scoreboard
posts.head: All three up. At the same time. Forever.
posts.sub: That’s what making money means. If one number rises while another falls, someone is playing games with the books.

posts.label: The problem
posts.text: Eddie, the night-shift supervisor, measures his whole world in the left column. Headquarters measures the right one. Nobody can say how a shift on the floor moves the money.

posts.label: Home · past midnight
posts.text: He forgot to call home. Again. Their date night, missed. His daughter Sharon waited up to show him her report card: straight A’s. His kid is acing second grade while he’s failing at business. He thinks about calling a headhunter. Then he decides he won’t run.

No budget for consultants. No time to go back to school. Just his own eyes, ears and mind. Lying awake next to his sleeping wife, Alex decides he has to find Jonah again. He has no idea where Jonah is.

chapters.title: The Midnight Call
chapters.hook: A dusty attic, an old address book, and a 3 AM call to London.
recap: Jonah’s three measures: throughput, inventory, operational expense.
The goal, restated: throughput up while inventory and operational expense go down.
The robots raised efficiency but piled up inventory and sold nothing more.

posts.head: He searches his mother’s attic for one phone number.
posts.sub: At 3:45 AM, the old phone on the stairs rings. It’s London.

posts.label: His old neighborhood · 8 PM
posts.text: After a day lost to meetings, Alex remembers his college address book. It must be at his mother’s. She opens the door and assumes someone has died. Hours in the attic and the basement turn up model airplanes, old love letters and the story of Uncle Paul’s embezzlement. The book is in his old desk, top drawer.

posts.label: The stairs · 1 AM to 3 AM
posts.text: He sits on the stairs with his mother’s ancient telephone and dials Israel, where it is already morning. A university friend gives him a number. That number gives him another. By three o’clock he knows where Jonah is: London. He leaves a message and dozes off next to the phone.

msgs.text: Alex. I presume you have something to tell me.
The goal of a manufacturing company is to make money. Everything else is a means.
Very good, Alex. Very good.
But down at the plant, profit and ROI tell me nothing about what happens on the floor.
That’s why I use three different measurements. Write them down.

posts.take: Throughput = money from sales. Inventory = money tied up in things to sell. Operational expense = money spent turning inventory into throughput.
posts.label: Jonah’s three measurements

items.text: Throughput: the rate the system makes money through sales. Not production: sales.
Inventory: all the money tied up in things the system intends to sell.
Operational expense: all the money spent turning inventory into throughput.

posts.text: Build something and fail to sell it, and it isn’t throughput. Jonah warns that the wording is precise: change one definition and you must change another.

posts.t: You decide: the goal in three numbers
posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Jonah hangs up before saying how the goal fits his measures. Which way should each one move?

options.text: All three up
options.feedback: Inventory and expense going up means more money stuck and spent.

options.text: Throughput up, inventory and operational expense down
options.feedback: That’s the answer Alex reaches.

options.text: Throughput steady, everything else down
options.feedback: Cutting alone can’t make a company grow.

posts.reveal: Driving home, Alex works it out: increase throughput while reducing inventory and operational expense, all at the same time. And Jonah’s three robot questions were exactly these measures in disguise.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.take: The goal on the floor: raise throughput while cutting inventory and operational expense.
posts.label: The big idea
posts.head: Throughput up. Inventory down. Expense down.
posts.sub: It’s the same goal, making money, stated in terms a plant can act on every day. All three moves, at the same time.

msgs.text: When the robots came on line, did sales go up?
Not even a blip. The only thing that went up is overdue shipments.
The robots were at 30% efficiency, so we released more material to keep them busy. Now every month ends with a surplus.
We’ve got piles of some parts and none of the parts they go with.
We haven’t been managing according to the goal.

posts.text: Alex has to explain to his staff why a physicist on the phone is about to change how they run the plant. Bob is skeptical. Lou wants proof. And before the day is out, Jonah will ask Alex to get on a plane that night.

chapters.title: Breakfast in New York
chapters.hook: One hotel breakfast, and the idea of a perfectly balanced factory falls apart.
recap: Every dollar is throughput, inventory or operational expense.
Keeping everyone busy is what piles up inventory.
Dependent events plus statistical fluctuations break the ‘balanced plant’.

posts.head: One breakfast with Jonah turns everything Alex knows about efficiency upside down.
posts.sub: And it starts with a question about idle workers.

posts.label: Conference room · afternoon
posts.text: Alex writes the three measurements on the whiteboard. Bob objects: why does throughput say sales? Marketing sells; they make things. Alex walks him to the window and points at the warehouses full of finished goods. Would the company survive just filling those? Bob gets it. Lou notices every definition is about money: coming in, stuck inside, going out.

posts.take: Money you could sell back is inventory; money you spend to make sales is operational expense.
posts.label: Lou’s rule of thumb
posts.text: Money still inside the system that could be sold is inventory. Money spent turning it into sales is expense.

posts.label: Home, then a hotel room
posts.text: Packing for the night flight, Alex gets no sympathy. Everything is for the job, Julie says, and the kids keep asking why he is like this. She might not be home when he calls. In New York he dials every fifteen minutes until two in the morning. Nobody picks up.

msgs.text: I don’t have time to solve your problems. But I think you can solve them yourself. I’ll give you rules.
What will this cost me?
Pay me the value of what you learn. If the plant closes, you owe nothing.
Now: a worker stands idle with nothing to do. Good or bad?
Bad. Always. It’s waste.
A plant where everybody is busy all the time is a very inefficient plant.

posts.t: You decide: where inventory comes from
posts.label: Jonah asks
posts.q: Your floor is buried in excess inventory. Where did it come from?

options.text: The market changed
options.feedback: Partly. But someone still had to make those parts.

options.text: Vendors sent bad batches
options.feedback: That causes delays, not piles of extra parts.

options.text: People and machines kept busy making things nobody needed yet
options.feedback: That’s Jonah’s point.

posts.reveal: Machines don’t run themselves. Excess inventory can only come from excess capacity kept busy. Jonah isn’t asking for layoffs; he is asking how Alex manages capacity.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.take: A perfectly balanced plant is a plant heading for trouble.
posts.myth: The perfect plant is balanced: every machine’s capacity matches demand exactly.
posts.truth: Trim every resource to exactly match demand and the plant drifts toward bankruptcy.

posts.label: Why balance fails

items.text: Dependent events: a step can’t start until the one before it is done.
Statistical fluctuations: how long each step takes varies, like waiting for a waiter to bring the check.

posts.text: Each one alone looks harmless. Jonah says the trouble is what they do together.

posts.label: Hotel lobby · 8:15 AM
posts.text: Then Jonah stands up: clients are waiting. He tells Alex to call back once he can explain what those two forces together mean for his plant. Alex, fuming, pays and follows him out. A man in a pinstripe suit leads Jonah to a black limousine. Inside waits a silver-haired executive, talking about a meeting with the chairman and the board.

Alex flies home with a riddle instead of answers. Dependent events. Statistical fluctuations. Together they do something to his plant, and he can’t see what. And there is a second question he can’t answer: where was Julie all night?

chapters.title: Into the Woods
chapters.hook: He promised his wife a great weekend. He’d already promised his son a Boy Scout hike.
recap: Julie and Alex make a deal: paperwork at home, evenings together.
On the hike, the line keeps stretching even at a steady average pace.
In a dependent line, delays pass down and speed can’t be stored up.

posts.head: He promised his wife a great weekend. His son had other plans.
posts.sub: Fifteen Boy Scouts, a 10-mile trail, and a line that keeps stretching, just like his factory.

posts.label: Home · Friday afternoon
posts.text: Julie is home. She spent the night with an old friend two hours away and talked until it was too late to drive. His career always comes first, she says; even at home he isn’t really there. They make a deal: he’ll bring his paperwork home in the evenings so the family at least sees him. And this weekend, he’s all hers.

posts.head: Saturday, 7 AM: a Boy Scout in the doorway.
posts.text: Davey is in full uniform. Dad promised to help the troopmaster on the overnight hike, remember? The gear is already packed. At the trailhead the troopmaster is out sick, the other parents drive off fast, and Alex is the only adult with fifteen boys and ten miles to Devil’s Gulch.

posts.label: On the trail · morning
posts.text: Alex walks at the back to watch everyone. Ron leads at a steady, average pace. Yet the column keeps stretching. Gaps open, then grow. Each time the line bunches behind Herbie on a hill, the front races half a mile ahead and the back has to run to catch up.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Everyone walks at about the same average speed. Why does the line keep getting longer?

options.text: Some kids are lazy
options.feedback: Nobody is slacking. Herbie is even running to keep up.

options.text: Slowdowns pile up, but nobody can go faster than the kid in front
options.feedback: That’s what Alex works out.

options.text: The map is wrong
options.feedback: The map is fine. Ron is right on pace.

posts.reveal: A kid can always slow down, but can only go as fast as the one ahead of him. So the slow moments add up instead of averaging out.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.take: In a dependent chain, delays accumulate; speed-ups are capped by the step ahead.
posts.label: The big idea
posts.head: Slowness piles up. Speed can’t.
posts.sub: When steps depend on each other, every delay passes down the line, but no one can make up time faster than the person ahead allows. That is dependent events plus statistical fluctuations.

posts.label: The hike is a factory
left: Energy spent running to catch up
posts.text: Inventory growing, throughput falling, expense rising: on the trail and in the plant.

posts.label: On the trail · noon
posts.text: Alex is about to decide it all averages out after all: the line in front of him has stopped stretching. Then he sees why. Ron isn’t walking anymore. He is standing at the side of the trail. It’s noon, the schedule says lunch, and they are still far short of the river where lunch was supposed to be.

Over lunch, Alex grabs a box of matches, some mess-kit bowls and one die, and invents a game for the boys. He expects it to prove that a perfectly balanced line runs smoothly. It is about to prove the opposite.

chapters.title: The Matchstick Game
chapters.hook: A bowl of matches and a single die explain why his plant is always late.
recap: Alex models a perfectly balanced plant with matches, bowls and a die.
Twenty matches came out instead of thirty-five; inventory piled up inside.
In a dependent chain, fluctuations accumulate instead of averaging out.

posts.head: Five boys, a box of matches and one die.
posts.sub: A game Alex invents to prove Jonah wrong ends up proving him right.

posts.label: Lunch break
posts.text: Maybe Jonah is simply wrong. If every station had exactly the capacity the market needs, wouldn’t the excess inventory vanish? Alex can’t clone fifteen identical scouts. But he can build a model: a row of bowls, a box of matches, and one die to decide how many matches each station can move.

posts.label: The rules

items.text: Five players, five bowls in a row: five dependent steps.
Roll the die and move that many matches to the next bowl.
You can only pass what is already in your bowl.
The average roll is 3.5, so ten rounds should push 35 matches out.

posts.text: Beat 3.5 a turn and you skip dishes tonight. Fall short and you scrub.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Every station is equal and the average roll is 3.5. After ten rounds, how many matches come out of the last bowl?

options.text: About 35
options.feedback: That’s what the boys expected.

options.text: More than 35, thanks to lucky rolls
options.feedback: Lucky rolls only help if there are matches to pass.

options.text: Far fewer than 35
options.feedback: Right. Brace for dishes.

posts.reveal: Only 20. The front of the line met its quota. Dave and Evan at the end sank deeper below quota every round: starved of matches, then buried when a pile finally arrived.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

msgs.text: Hey, keep those matches coming down here!
I’m doing my job up here. What’s wrong with you guys?
I finally get some matches and I roll a one.
If I wash dishes because you didn’t give me matches…
Evan, I’d start warming up on the spaghetti pot.

posts.take: Balanced line, average 3.5 a turn: only 20 of 35 matches came out.
posts.label: Mr. Rogo’s score sheet
posts.text: A perfectly balanced system, and it still failed its customers.

posts.myth: Lucky and unlucky streaks cancel out over time.
posts.truth: In a chain of dependent steps, losses pile up downstream and upstream gains go to waste.

posts.take: In a dependent chain, inventory moves in waves and the end of the line falls behind.
posts.label: Why balance fails
posts.head: Inventory moves in waves.
posts.sub: Matches don’t flow; they bunch up in one bowl, then flood the next. The further down the line, the bigger the swings, and the further behind schedule the whole system falls.

posts.label: Alex, at the table
posts.text: Half the orders late. Delivery dates nobody can promise. Customers losing faith. Alex looks at the chart and recognizes his own plant. The boys play twenty more rounds; the chart plunges deeper and deeper. Then it is time to hit the trail again, and Herbie is still at the back.
Back on the trail, the column stretches faster than ever, and they are hours behind schedule. Alex looks at Herbie, the slowest kid in the woods, and has an idea that sounds completely backwards.

chapters.title: Herbie
chapters.hook: Halfway through the hike they’re crawling at one mile an hour. So Alex puts the slowest kid in front.
recap: The troop can move no faster than its slowest walker.
Alex puts Herbie in front, and nobody passes anybody.
Lighten Herbie’s pack and the whole troop doubles its speed.

posts.head: Halfway there, and the troop is moving at one mile an hour.
posts.sub: So Alex puts the slowest kid in the woods at the front of the line.

posts.label: Back of the line
posts.text: Walking at the back, Alex works out why the matchstick plant failed: there was no reserve. When a station fell behind, it had no spare capacity to catch up, so every shortfall became the next station’s starting point. Up ahead, the gaps are widening again. The boys have quietly reshuffled the line, and Alex finds himself stuck behind one kid. Herbie.

posts.take: A chain of dependent steps moves at the speed of its slowest step.
posts.label: The insight
posts.head: The troop is only as fast as Herbie.
posts.sub: It doesn’t matter how fast the leader walks. The troop arrives when its slowest walker arrives. Herbie’s pace is the troop’s throughput; the stretched-out line is its inventory.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Herbie is the slowest walker, and the whole troop is waiting on him. You’re Alex. What do you do?

options.text: Keep him at the back so he slows nobody down
options.feedback: That’s where he was. The line stretched for a mile.

options.text: Tell everyone to hurry up
options.feedback: The gaps close for a few minutes, then open again.

options.text: Put Herbie in front and let nobody pass
options.feedback: That’s Alex’s call.

posts.reveal: Alex takes Herbie by the hand and leads him past the whole column until the order is reversed. New rule: nobody passes anybody. The fast kids groan. But the gaps close and stay closed.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

msgs.text: You want HIM to lead? He’s the slowest one!
Exactly. Everybody keeps up with the kid in front. Nobody passes.
Mr. Rogo, I’m falling asleep back here.
Want to go faster? Then figure out how Herbie can go faster.
Hey, Herbie, what’s in your pack?
None of your business!

posts.take: The fix wasn’t speeding up the fast kids. It was taking weight off the slowest one.
posts.label: Alex opens it
posts.h: What the slowest kid was carrying
posts.text: ‘We’re supposed to be prepared,’ Herbie says. Alex, the biggest, takes most of it. Herbie goes back to the front.

posts.head: Twice as fast. Still together.
posts.text: Freed of the weight, Herbie practically flies. The troop moves at double its old speed and no gap opens. They reach Devil’s Gulch at five: about four miles in two hours, after crawling at one mile an hour all day.

posts.take: Speeding up anyone but the slowest step just builds inventory.
posts.myth: If every person goes as fast as they can, the group goes as fast as it can.
posts.truth: A fast walker up front only stretches the line. The group’s speed is its slowest member’s speed, so the only speed-up that counts is his.

posts.label: Devil’s Gulch · that night
posts.text: The wilderness turns out to overlook a shopping center. Herbie asks if it has a Burger King. Dave and Evan cook the spaghetti. Later, in their tent, Dave goes quiet, then says he was really proud of his dad today: the way he figured it out, kept everyone together, and put Herbie in front.
Sunday, 4:30 PM. Father and son pull into the driveway, sunburned and pleased with themselves. Julie’s car is gone. Inside, a closet door in the bedroom is standing open.

chapters.title: Last in Line
chapters.hook: Julie leaves a note. His rival gets promoted over him. And a ten-dollar bet proves Jonah right on the factory floor.
recap: Julie leaves: she is tired of always coming last for Alex.
Hilton Smyth becomes division productivity manager.
A rush job proves it: the robot finished 10 pieces short of 100.

posts.head: Most of her clothes are gone. There’s an envelope on the kitchen table.
posts.sub: And on Monday, a robot loses him a ten-dollar bet and wins him an argument.

posts.label: The bedroom
posts.text: Julie’s note is short. She is tired of always coming last for him, and she has decided he won’t change. She is going away for a while to think. She is sorry; she knows he’s busy. And she has left Sharon with his mother. He has spent the weekend learning what happens to whoever is last in line.

posts.label: The car, driving home from Grandma’s

msgs.text: Is Mommy still mad at me?
Mad at you? She isn’t mad at you.
Yes she is. She wouldn’t talk to me.
Sharon, you didn’t do anything wrong.
Then why?

posts.label: Monday, 9:15 AM
posts.text: Dave tries pancakes; they end up on the floor. Sharon says she’s too sick for school. Alex gets to work late, and Hilton Smyth is on the phone: Bearington owes his plant 100 sub-assemblies. All 100 by tonight, not 99, or he calls Peach. And maybe, Smyth adds sweetly, Alex should read his mail.

posts.head: His rival just got promoted.
posts.text: A memo from Peach: Hilton Smyth is the new division productivity manager. Every plant manager now reports to him on a dotted line, with special attention to cost reduction.

posts.label: Conference room · two hours of diagrams
posts.h: Alex explains the hike. The verdict:

items.text: Bob: on the fence. Robots don’t fluctuate.
Ralph: not sure what he’s hearing
Lou: you learned this from kids on a hike?

posts.text: One sympathizer, one undecided, one bewildered, one skeptic. Then Smyth’s rush job gives Alex an idea: let the plant prove it.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Pete’s department makes about 25 parts an hour, noon to four. The robot welds exactly 25 an hour, one to five. Smyth needs 100 on the five o’clock truck. Do they make it?

options.text: Yes. Both run at 25 an hour.
options.feedback: Bob took that side of the bet.

options.text: Yes, if Pete’s people hustle at the end
options.feedback: They did hustle. It wasn’t enough.

options.text: No
options.feedback: That’s Alex’s ten dollars.

posts.reveal: Pete’s crew finishes all 100 by four and walks out cheering, ‘We beat the robot!’ At five past five, the robot is still welding. The truck leaves without them.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.take: Pete made 100 on average. The robot could only weld what reached it: 90.
posts.label: Pete’s log + the robot’s log
posts.text: Every slow hour upstream passed straight to the robot. Pete’s fast hours were capped at 25. Pete was never more than 10 behind. They ended exactly 10 short.

posts.take: In a dependent chain, the biggest upstream shortfall caps what comes out the end.
posts.label: The lesson
posts.head: Upstream’s worst slump becomes downstream’s starting line.
posts.sub: Fluctuations don’t cancel out in a chain; the step after can’t recover what it never received. And Pete’s people felt like heroes for a job that didn’t ship. The incentives reward the wrong thing.

posts.text: Tuesday morning the staff stop doubting and start asking: how do you control a plant with fifty million variables? They call Jonah. On a ten-minute break from a lecture, he gives them one word to hunt for. Then he hangs up.

chapters.title: Hello, Herbie
chapters.hook: They went looking for the factory’s Herbie. They found two, stuck in the middle of the line.
recap: A bottleneck: any resource whose capacity is equal to or less than the demand on it.
Balance the flow through the plant with demand, not the capacity.
Two bottlenecks found: the NCX-10 and heat-treat. They can’t be moved or bought around.

posts.head: They went looking for the factory’s Herbie.
posts.sub: They found two, stuck in the middle of the line, and no money to fix either.

posts.label: Home · evening
posts.text: Sharon meets him at the door, beaming: Mommy called. She told the kids she loves them and will be away for a while. Davey asked for a number. She wouldn’t give one. At dinner, Alex’s mother, who has moved in with half her kitchen, tells Depression stories about how lucky they are to have food.

posts.label: Alex’s office · Jonah on a ten-minute break

msgs.text: A bottleneck is any resource whose capacity is equal to or less than the demand placed on it.
So where does market demand come in?
Don’t balance capacity with demand. Balance the flow of product with demand.
I thought bottlenecks were bad.
They’re a reality. Use them to control the flow. Do you have any?
We don’t know.
Then find out. Call me when you know.

posts.take: Balance flow, not capacity.
posts.myth: A well-run plant matches every resource’s capacity to demand, so nothing sits idle.
posts.truth: Balance the flow through the bottleneck with demand. Everything else needs spare capacity to absorb fluctuations.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Ralph’s data is a mess: the routings list machines the plant sold a year ago. Checking everything could take months. They have ten weeks. How do you find the bottleneck fast?

options.text: Fix the database first, then calculate
options.feedback: Garbage in, garbage out, and months of it.

options.text: Ask the people who chase late parts
options.feedback: Stacey’s idea. Good one.

options.text: Look for the biggest pile of waiting work
options.feedback: Alex’s idea. On the trail, gaps were inventory.

posts.reveal: They use every shortcut: Bob’s twenty years of hunches, the expediters’ list of parts they’re always chasing, and the biggest pile of work-in-process in the plant. Ralph checks the shortlist against the data.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.head: Herbie is the best machine in the plant.
posts.text: The NCX-10: the plant’s most efficient machine, with weeks of backlog stacked around it. Expediters are always waiting on it. Its operator wears earplugs to block out the complaints. And training a new setup person takes six months.

posts.label: Why the best machine is the bottleneck
posts.h: Cheaper per part. Less in total.
posts.text: Ten old machines working side by side out-produced one fast machine. The NCX-10 won on cost per part and lost on capacity.

posts.label: Heat-treat
posts.text: Two grimy furnaces at 1,500 degrees, cooking parts for six to sixteen hours a batch. They often run half empty, because expediters keep demanding a handful of parts for one shipment. A request for a third furnace was killed years ago for ‘low efficiencies.’ The staff are blunt: they can’t move either bottleneck to the front, and there is no money to buy around them.

posts.label: No money, no time
posts.q: Two bottlenecks stuck mid-line, and no budget for new machines. What would you do?

options.text: Ask headquarters for a second NCX-10 anyway
options.feedback: Lou: for a plant losing money, in this year? Out of our minds.

options.text: Rearrange the plant to put them first
options.feedback: Already ruled out. The sequence can’t change.

options.text: Find capacity hidden in the bottlenecks themselves
options.feedback: Hold that thought.

options.text: Accept it. The plant can’t be saved
options.feedback: That’s how the staff feels tonight.

posts.reveal: Jonah thinks there’s a way, and he is changing planes to show them. The answer arrives in Chapter 11.
posts.hint: Pick your answer. We’ll keep it for later.

posts.text: On the phone from Boston, Jonah says there are only two ways his ideas fail: no demand, or a manager who has decided not to change. Then he asks a strange question. Does Bearington have an airport?

chapters.title: The $2,735 Hour
chapters.hook: The plant’s most precious machine is idle. Jonah does the math: every hour like this costs $2,735.
recap: An hour lost at a bottleneck is an hour lost for the entire plant.
The true cost of a bottleneck hour: the plant’s total expense divided by the bottleneck’s hours.
Don’t buy capacity; stop wasting it, and move work off the bottlenecks.

posts.head: The plant’s most precious machine is standing idle.
posts.sub: Jonah takes one look and asks a question that costs $2,735 an hour.

posts.label: Dinner, before the airport
posts.text: Alex explains to the kids: the plant has two Herbies, stuck in the middle of the line. ‘So make them go faster,’ says Sharon. Dave remembers the hike: when Dad took Herbie’s pack, he flew. ‘It’s not that simple,’ Alex says. His mother has advice too: keep after them and make sure they don’t waste any more time.

msgs.text: This is your bottleneck. Why isn’t it working right now?
Setup crew went on break ten minutes ago. Back in twenty.
On a non-bottleneck, who cares when breaks happen? On a bottleneck, it’s the opposite.
It has about 585 hours a month available.
And demand is even higher. Lose an hour here and the whole plant loses it. Forever.

posts.head: The backup machines are gone.
posts.text: Jonah asks: the older machines the NCX-10 replaced, are they still around? One whole class of them was sold off, to free floor space for a new pen to store inventory.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: About a thousand parts sit waiting for heat-treat. Lou guesses $10–15 thousand in materials. What is that pile really worth?

options.text: About $15,000: the cost of the parts
options.feedback: Lou’s answer, and Stacey’s.

options.text: About $20,000 with materials and labor
options.feedback: Still thinking like an accountant.

options.text: About a million dollars
options.feedback: That’s Jonah’s number.

posts.reveal: Each part lets them finish and ship a product that sells for about $1,000. A thousand parts: a million dollars, if they get through heat-treat before customers give up and go elsewhere.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.take: Make sure a bottleneck only ever works on good parts.
posts.myth: Check quality just before final assembly, where you can see the whole product.
posts.truth: Inspect before the bottleneck. Scrap a part there and you lose a part. Scrap it afterwards and you lose bottleneck time you can never get back.

posts.take: An hour lost at a bottleneck costs what an hour of the entire plant costs.
posts.label: Lou’s calculator
posts.h: What an hour of the NCX-10 costs
posts.text: The plant produces what its bottleneck produces. So an idle bottleneck hour idles the whole plant: total expense divided by bottleneck hours.

posts.take: Increase bottleneck capacity by not wasting it and by offloading it.
posts.label: The answer
posts.head: Don’t buy capacity. Stop wasting it.
posts.sub: The capacity is already there, leaking away. Every bottleneck hour spent on the right part is an hour the whole plant earns. Protect those hours, and move work off the bottlenecks wherever you can.

posts.label: Before Jonah leaves
posts.h: How to stop wasting a bottleneck

items.text: No idle breaks: someone always runs it
Inspect quality in front of it
Only parts for orders due now, not months from now
Parts that don’t need it go elsewhere
Other machines or outside vendors take some load

posts.text: Building stock you can’t sell for months trades today’s cash for future cash. This plant can’t afford that.
At breakfast, Sharon mentions something she heard behind Mom’s voice on the phone: violins, the sleepy music Grandpa Barnett always plays. Julie’s parents swore they hadn’t heard from her.

chapters.title: Red Tags
chapters.hook: They gave the bottleneck a priority list. It stopped dead. The fix is a sticky label in two colors.
recap: Bottlenecks now work only on overdue orders, most overdue first.
Red tags mark bottleneck parts; everyone works on red before green.
Alex finds Julie at her parents’ house. She agrees to a date.

posts.head: They gave the bottleneck a priority list. It stopped dead.
posts.sub: The fix turns out to be a label in two colors.

posts.label: Julie’s parents’ house · sunset
posts.text: Julie’s mother finally admits it on the phone: Julie is there, and won’t talk to him. That evening Alex drives to Forest Grove. Her Accord sits in the driveway. Ada locks the screen door and threatens to call the police. ‘Then I’ll wait in my car,’ he says. ‘You don’t own the street.’ Forty-five minutes later, Julie walks out.

msgs.text: I don’t know if I want to be married to you anymore.
So do you want a divorce?
I don’t know yet. Everyone except me knows what I should do.
Come home. I promise we can make it better.
I’ve heard too many promises, Al.
You know, I do happen to love you.

posts.label: Staff meeting · 10 AM

items.text: Quality inspector in front of the bottlenecks, by tonight
New break rules so the bottlenecks never stop (union permitting)
Late orders first: two weeks late beats one week late
Bottlenecks work only on parts for those late orders

posts.text: Lou rechecked overnight: only 80% of products pass through a bottleneck, so the real cost is $2,188 an hour, not $2,735. ‘Still an eye-opener,’ he admits.

posts.label: Next morning · conference room
posts.text: Stacey and Ralph worked most of the night. There are 67 overdue orders; the worst is 58 days late. About 90% need parts from a bottleneck. The supervisors of heat-treat and the NCX-10 get one instruction: start at the top of the list and work down. Nothing else. Stacey makes Alex promise not to bend it for marketing.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: The NCX-10 crew finishes the first two jobs on the list. The material for the third is nowhere to be found. What should they do?

options.text: Wait for it. The list says in order.
options.feedback: That’s what they did. The NCX-10 sat idle.

options.text: Skip to the next job they have material for
options.feedback: What Alex meant. Nobody said it.

options.text: Run whatever is handy to stay busy
options.feedback: That’s how the plant got here.

posts.reveal: They waited. The missing parts had been sitting for a week at a lathe, where the foreman was busy with a long run of ordinary parts. To him the small bottleneck batch looked unimportant. Nobody had told him otherwise.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.take: A worker who can’t tell urgent from routine will stay busy on the wrong thing.
posts.label: The lesson
posts.head: Busy and helpful are not the same.
posts.sub: The lathe foreman was doing his job: stay busy, never break a long run. That rule just held up a shipment. ‘I had to break all the rules,’ says Bob. ‘Then the rules had to be broken,’ says Alex.

posts.label: The new system
right: Only when no red is waiting
posts.text: Every shift gets a fifteen-minute briefing, with an hourglass to explain why, and a new plant newsletter to follow up.

posts.label: Friday · then Saturday, 7:29 PM
posts.text: The union calls: go ahead with the new break rules, no challenge. And on Saturday at 7:29, a washed and waxed Mazda pulls into the Barnetts’ driveway. Alex has flowers and new clothes. ‘Well, don’t you look nice,’ says Julie. He jokes that he’ll have her home by ten. ‘Good,’ says her mother. ‘We’ll be waiting.’
A week later, the shipments are better. Alex isn’t satisfied. Then Bob calls, sounding like a kid on Christmas morning: meet me on the receiving dock. Something big is arriving under a tarp.

chapters.title: The Zmegma
chapters.hook: Bob whips a tarp off a machine older than anyone in the room. It might save the plant.
recap: Red tags work: twelve of the most overdue orders ship in a week.
Old machines and dedicated crews add capacity to the bottlenecks.
Slowing some non-bottlenecks removes 20% of the furnace load.

posts.head: Bob whips the tarp off and shouts, ‘Ta-da!’
posts.sub: Underneath is a machine older than anyone in the room. It might just save the plant.

posts.take: The bottleneck-first system worked in week one, but not fast enough.
posts.label: Ralph’s printout

items.text: Taken from the top of the list
Bad parts caught before the NCX-10

posts.text: ‘It isn’t enough,’ Alex says. ‘We shouldn’t have any late orders.’ He wants plans to offload the bottlenecks by Wednesday.

posts.label: Alex’s office
posts.text: A part leaving a bottleneck looks almost identical to one going in. But one has used up irreplaceable bottleneck time. The communications manager has an idea: a strip of yellow tape on the red tag after the bottleneck. It tells everyone on sight to treat that part like gold. Quality starts writing special procedures for those parts.

msgs.text: It’s a Zmegma! They don’t build ’em like this anymore.
Glad to hear it. That was state of the art around 1942.
With a Screwmeister and that machine in the corner, it does everything the NCX-10 does.
The kind we sold to make room for inventory?
Yep. A buddy at our South End plant gave us one. Cost: the truck rental.
Does it still work?

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Ralph’s math says the bottlenecks made enough parts for 18 to 20 shipments last week. They shipped 12. The NCX-10 numbers check out. What’s wrong?

options.text: Ralph’s math is off
options.feedback: He checked twice.

options.text: Finished parts are sitting in the furnace
options.feedback: Ralph caught it with a stopwatch.

options.text: Too many defects
options.feedback: Quality now catches those before the bottleneck.

posts.reveal: Ralph timed a heat himself. Parts due out at 3 PM were still inside at 5:30; they came out around eight. The helpers had been sent to other jobs. Down there, that happens all the time.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.label: Wednesday staff meeting
posts.h: Find the capacity, then the people

items.text: A machinist and helper stationed at the NCX-10, all three shifts
A foreman and two helpers at the furnaces, all three shifts
Zmegma and two old machines, one shift a day: +18% NCX-10 output
Surplus heat-treat work sent to a vendor across town

posts.text: There’s a hiring freeze. So they take people from non-bottlenecks, which have spare capacity by definition. ‘From now on,’ says Alex, ‘only our best people work on the bottlenecks.’

posts.label: Heat-treat · 6 AM
posts.text: Mike Haley, the third-shift foreman, is pushing 10% more through the furnaces than anyone. His helpers pre-sort parts into stacks by temperature, so a furnace that needs only fifty parts for one late order gets topped up with other parts that run at the same heat. His next idea: tables that roll in and out on a forklift, so a load change takes minutes instead of an hour. Alex moves him to day shift to write it all down.

posts.head: Some of those parts never needed heat-treat.
posts.text: Five years ago, someone sped up three non-bottleneck machines by cutting deeper on each pass. That made the metal brittle, so the parts needed heat-treat. Slow those machines back down and about 20% of the furnace load disappears. No engineering approval needed; the plant made the change itself.

posts.take: Local efficiency on a non-bottleneck can steal capacity from the bottleneck.
posts.myth: Every machine should run as efficiently as it possibly can.
posts.truth: Making three non-bottlenecks ‘efficient’ created a fifth of the work on a bottleneck. Slow them down and the whole plant goes faster.

posts.text: A Friday afternoon, a few weeks later. Something goes BAM off the ceiling tiles of Alex’s office. It’s a champagne cork, and half the plant is crowding through his door.

chapters.title: Champagne
chapters.hook: The best month in the plant’s history. A midnight misunderstanding. And a new problem nobody saw coming.
recap: Record month: 57 orders, about $3 million, inventory down 12%.
Julie misreads a late night; Stacey sets it straight.
Ordinary green-tag parts start going missing at assembly.

posts.head: BAM. A champagne cork ricochets off his ceiling.
posts.sub: The best month in the plant’s history, and a night that could end his marriage.

posts.take: Shipments nearly doubled while inventory fell.
posts.label: Lou checked the books

items.text: Old record, orders in a month

posts.text: ‘Then let’s drink to making money,’ says Alex. Bob’s champagne comes by the case and, in Stacey’s words, is industrial strength.

msgs.text: I was just talking to Johnny Jons.
What’s the problem?
No problem. He’s happy. You’ve been coming through on a lot of late orders.
I’m always on your case when things go wrong, Al. So: thanks, from me and Jons.
Thanks, Bill. Thanks for calling.

posts.label: Alex’s front door
posts.text: The party moves to dinner, then a bar. Stacey, on club soda for hours, drives Alex home. At the door he goes to shake her hand, trips over the step, and they both end up on the floor, laughing so hard they cry. Then the lights come on.

posts.head: Julie.
posts.text: She drove over on impulse because she missed him and the kids, then waited six hours with his mother. Now she finds him drunk on the floor, laughing with a woman she has never met. She reverses out of the garage at thirty miles an hour.

posts.label: Monday morning
posts.text: Stacey offers to call Julie and explain. Then she shows Alex something worse. An order of 200 units needed 172 different parts; 17 were missing. Only one had a red tag, and it came out of heat-treat on time. The other sixteen were ordinary green-tag parts, and they still haven’t shown up. Vendors aren’t the problem. It’s inside the plant.

posts.label: Something’s wrong
posts.q: Bottleneck parts now arrive on time. Ordinary parts don’t. What’s going on?

options.text: Higher sales have created new bottlenecks
options.feedback: Stacey’s theory. Sounds right.

options.text: Suppliers are shipping late
options.feedback: Stacey already checked. They aren’t.

options.text: The red-tag priority system itself
options.feedback: Interesting. Hold that thought.

options.text: People are slacking off
options.feedback: Nobody on the floor is idle.

posts.reveal: On the phone, Jonah asks Alex to list everything they’ve changed. He stops at one item: ‘New priority system?’ Then he says he had better come have another look. The answer arrives in Chapter 15.
posts.hint: Pick your answer. We’ll keep it for later.

posts.label: The floor
posts.text: A month ago, the aisles were canyons of half-finished parts. Last week, for the first time since he came to this plant, Alex walked to the assembly line without turning sideways. He took it as a good sign.

msgs.text: I owe you an apology. Stacey called me. I completely misunderstood.
There’s been a lot of misunderstanding between us lately.
I drove down thinking you’d be glad to see me.
I would have been, if you’d stayed. Friends again?
Yes. When will I see you?

posts.text: Next morning, Jonah walks out of Gate Two again. Within an hour he is kneeling on the factory floor with a piece of chalk, about to explain why their best idea created their newest problem.

chapters.title: Drum and Rope
chapters.hook: The plant’s new bottleneck isn’t a bottleneck. And a second-grader works out the fix at the kitchen table.
recap: A non-bottleneck’s useful work is set by the bottleneck, not by its own capacity.
Activating a resource is not the same as utilizing it.
Release material only at the pace the bottlenecks can use it.

posts.head: Their newest bottleneck isn’t a bottleneck. They built it.
posts.sub: Jonah explains with chalk on the floor. A second-grader finishes the job at the kitchen table.

posts.label: The milling machines · 10:30 AM
posts.text: Thirty parts are missing. Most of them are right here, under green tags, untouched for two or three weeks. The foreman shrugs: he’s following the rules. Red first. And 75 to 80% of everything that reaches heat-treat or the NCX-10 passes through his machines first. The red parts never stop coming, so the green ones never get a turn.

msgs.text: So what now? Switch the missing parts to red?
I guess the only answer is to expedite.
Expedite now and you’ll be expediting forever. Come look at your bottleneck.
How do we even get to it?
A month of work, I’d guess, and every piece with a red tag. Why is it all here?

posts.label: Jonah’s chalk diagrams
left: The extra piles up at X
right: Y’s parts wait for X’s parts
posts.text: In every combination, Y never sets throughput. Running it beyond what X or the market can absorb makes one thing: inventory.

posts.take: Releasing material to keep everyone busy can create a bottleneck that wasn’t there.
posts.label: The answer
posts.head: You turned the milling machines into a bottleneck.
posts.sub: Every time a non-bottleneck ran out of work, more material went onto the floor. Throughput only rose 20%; the flood of releases is what swamped the mills. The red parts took every hour, and the green ones waited.

posts.take: Activating a resource and utilizing it are not the same thing.
posts.myth: A machine that’s running is a machine that’s being productive.
posts.truth: Activating a resource just means switching it on. Utilizing it means work that moves the plant toward the goal. A system of local optimums is not an optimum system.

posts.label: Sharon and Dave’s puzzle
posts.q: Herbie is stuck in the middle of the line and can’t move. The kids ahead of him keep walking faster, and the line spreads out. How do you keep it together?

options.text: A drummer, and Herbie beats the drum
options.feedback: Sharon’s answer, like a parade.

options.text: Tie everyone together with one rope
options.feedback: Dave’s answer, like mountain climbers.

options.text: Just keep the front kid from outpacing Herbie
options.feedback: The simplest version of both.

posts.reveal: Both kids were close. You don’t need everyone in step, or everyone tied. Just keep the kid at the front from walking faster than Herbie. Their prize? Sharon asks for one thing: get Mom to come home.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.label: Ralph’s idea
posts.h: Let the bottleneck call for material

items.text: Ralph can predict weeks ahead what each bottleneck will work on
Material takes about two weeks to reach a bottleneck
Release red material only as fast as the bottleneck uses it
Keep about three days of work waiting in front of it
Time every other release backwards from assembly

posts.text: The bottlenecks now decide when material enters the plant. It works like putting Herbie at the front, without moving a single machine.

posts.label: Next morning
posts.text: Bob raises a red flag: if they hold material back, people will be idle and efficiencies will drop, right before Peach decides the plant’s fate. Stacey answers: a person already on the payroll costs nothing extra standing still; excess inventory ties up real money. Alex decides. They go ahead, and if efficiencies drop, let them.

End of May, headquarters. The division’s numbers man announces that Bearington alone kept the division from a seventh straight monthly loss. Alex waits for Peach’s reaction. Peach says two words. Then he says something much harder.

chapters.title: Four Weeks
chapters.hook: The best report in the division earns two words from Peach, and a demand for 15% more.
recap: Bearington gives the division its first operating profit of the year.
Peach wants 15% more on the bottom line, and the overdue backlog is gone.
Jonah: halve batch sizes. Lead times shrink from months to weeks.

posts.head: The best report in the division. Peach says ‘good job’ and asks for 15% more.
posts.sub: Then Jonah calls from Singapore with an idea that seems to make everything cost more.

posts.label: 15th floor · monthly review
posts.text: The division’s numbers man says it plainly: without Bearington, the division would have lost money for a seventh straight month. Ralph’s new system now predicts each shipment to within a day. The overdue backlog is gone. Peach, with Smyth whispering at his side, says only, ‘Good job.’ Alex decides not to tell him everything yet. They have broken too many rules.

msgs.text: So when are you going to let us off the hook?
What makes you think I’m going to? You had a huge backlog. Shipping it was inevitable.
If we improve again next month, will you hold off on closing us?
Give me fifteen percent more on the bottom line than this month.
I think we can do that.
Then keep delivering it, and Bearington stays open.

posts.head: He just promised orders he doesn’t have.
posts.text: Speeding home, it hits him. Last month looked great because they finally shipped the overdue backlog. That’s gone now, and new orders are going out much faster than they come in. Where will an extra 15% come from?

posts.label: A park bench by the river
posts.text: Julie says she’s still afraid that if she comes home, the same fights will start within a week. Alex asks what their marriage is supposed to be for. ‘When you’re married, you’re just married,’ she says. ‘There is no goal.’ They walk back like two icebergs. Then she runs after his car: Saturday? ‘We’ll keep trying until we get it right.’

posts.take: Most of a part’s time in a plant is spent waiting, and the bottlenecks set that waiting.
posts.label: Jonah, calling from Singapore
posts.h: A part’s life inside the plant

items.text: Queue: waiting for a busy machine

posts.text: Jonah’s next step: cut batch sizes in half on non-bottlenecks. Half the batch, roughly half the sitting.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Half-size batches mean twice as many setups. Bob protests: setups cost money. What do you tell him?

options.text: He’s right. Keep the big batches.
options.feedback: On paper, yes. In cash, no.

options.text: Halve batches only on the bottlenecks
options.feedback: Backwards. Bottleneck time is the precious kind.

options.text: Extra setups on non-bottlenecks are free
options.feedback: That’s the argument Alex makes.

posts.reveal: Jonah’s rule: an hour saved at a non-bottleneck is a mirage. Material is now held back, so non-bottlenecks have idle time. Extra setups just use some of it. Nobody is hired. Nothing extra is spent.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.take: Smaller batches shrink lead time, and short lead time wins business.
posts.label: The payoff
posts.head: Half the batch, half the wait.
posts.sub: Lead time was three to four months; the new priorities cut it to about two. Halve the batches and it could be four weeks. Customers get orders sooner, and sales can promise what competitors can’t.

msgs.text: Four weeks? Last winter we promised four months and took six!
Get me ten orders and I’ll prove it.
And what happens to our credibility if you can’t?
If I miss four weeks, I’ll buy you a new pair of Guccis.
Deal. We’ll offer six weeks. Ship in under five and I’ll buy YOU shoes.

posts.text: 4:20 AM. In a nightmare, Peach chases him through the aisles in his crimson Mercedes, yelling that the bottom line isn’t good enough. Alex wakes next to Julie. New orders are coming in. But one number has gone the wrong way.

chapters.title: A Thousand Model 12s
chapters.hook: A thousand units in two weeks, a million dollars, and an order a competitor sat on for five months.
recap: Smaller batches: efficiencies up and inventory at its lowest ever.
On paper, more setups make each part look more expensive.
Burnside wants 1,000 units in two weeks. Alex offers 250 a week, and wins.

posts.head: A thousand units. Two weeks. A million dollars.
posts.sub: An order a competitor sat on for five months, for a customer who swore off Bearington.

posts.label: The house in Bearington
posts.text: With the kids at Julie’s parents, the two of them had the empty house to themselves: wine, cheese, a loaf of bread. Now Alex stands at the dark window, wide awake. Most of yesterday’s staff meeting was good news. One part wasn’t.

posts.label: Yesterday’s staff meeting

items.text: About half a dozen new orders since the Gucci bet
Inventory at its lowest ever, half its old size
Idle time comes in ten-minute pieces, not two-hour ones

posts.text: Smaller batches move to the next station sooner, so fewer machines sit starved waiting for a huge batch to finish.

msgs.text: How come you’re out here in the dark?
Our cost measurements.
I thought everything was getting better.
It is. Politically it’s bad. Financially it doesn’t make a bit of difference.
Then tell me about it.

posts.take: Cost accounting assumes every worker is always busy, so extra setups look like extra cost.
posts.label: A pencil and paper at dawn
posts.text: Overhead is calculated from labor, so it rises on paper too. In reality nobody was hired and nothing extra was spent. More product now shares the same costs, so real cost per part went down.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Lou can calculate costs from the last two months instead of the last twelve. It’s more realistic, but it breaks accounting policy, and headquarters would catch it if they looked. Do it?

options.text: Yes. It buys time.
options.feedback: That’s Alex’s call.

options.text: No. Report by the book.
options.feedback: Then Peach sees costs rising. Hot water either way.

posts.reveal: Alex takes the risk. ‘Remember, if we get caught…’ Lou warns. Alex says he’ll practice his tap dancing. Then Fran buzzes: Johnny Jons is on the line.
posts.hint: Pick one. Then see what Alex did.

msgs.text: Remember our dear friend Bucky Burnside? He wants a thousand Model 12s.
Terrific!
By the end of the month. We have fifty in the warehouse.
That’s two weeks.
Our biggest competitor had the order five months and can’t deliver. Come through and we could be their preferred supplier.

posts.label: Alex’s office · all morning
posts.text: Ralph: the bottlenecks can make parts for about 100 units a day, but only if every other customer waits. No. So: halve the batch sizes again. Hold orders scheduled to ship early until their due dates. Stacey finds the control modules in California, four to six weeks out, so they ask for weekly shipments by air freight. On a million-dollar sale, freight is small change.

posts.take: Splitting a big order into regular smaller shipments can make the impossible deliverable.
posts.label: The offer
posts.head: 250 a week beats 1,000 at once.
posts.sub: Starting two weeks after the order: 250 units a week for four weeks. Nobody else’s order slips. Burnside not only accepts, he likes the smaller shipments better.

posts.text: That evening Jons shouts down the phone: we got it! A million dollars rings up in Alex’s other ear. The first 250 ship in two weeks. At headquarters, though, someone is about to look very closely at Lou’s numbers.

chapters.title: The Helicopter
chapters.hook: An audit wipes out his best number. Then a helicopter lands on the front lawn.
recap: The month comes in at 17%: inventory down 60%, throughput doubled.
An audit restores the old cost rules: on paper, only 12.8%.
Burnside flies in to thank everyone. Alex and Julie decide to marry again.

posts.head: The audit wiped out his best number. Then a helicopter landed on the lawn.
posts.sub: Out stepped the toughest customer in the business.

posts.take: Seventeen percent: more than Peach asked for.
posts.label: Lou, late to the staff meeting
posts.text: Two letters arrive from Peach: congratulations on Burnside, and notice of a formal plant review at headquarters.

posts.label: C-aisle · while Alex is away
posts.text: Hilton Smyth shows up with a TV crew to film a video about robot productivity. One problem: the robot has nothing to do. No inventory anywhere near it. Bob spends an hour hunting for parts it can stack. Meanwhile a bored Smyth wanders the floor, asking a lot of questions about batch sizes.

posts.head: 17% becomes 12.8%.
posts.text: Two days later, auditors from the division take over the conference room. They find the changed cost base within hours. ‘Highly irregular.’ Recalculated by the old standards, costs appear to rise, and the gain shrinks to 12.8%. Peach says nothing.

posts.label: Alex’s office · early afternoon
posts.text: A red and white helicopter settles on the lawn. Out climbs Johnny Jons, and a huge, white-haired man with a swagger: Bucky Burnside. Alex sprints to Stacey: was the last shipment on time? Yes. He finds Bob in the men’s room: any quality problems? None. ‘Clockwork.’ Then what is Burnside doing here?

msgs.text: Rogo! I came to shake the hand of every employee in your plant.
The other outfit sat on our order five months. Your people did it in five weeks. Must have been an incredible effort!
We just did our best.
Won’t hurt your efficiency, will it?
Not one bit. Go right ahead.

posts.t: Did they pull out all the stops?
posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Burnside thinks the plant moved heaven and earth. Did it?

options.text: Yes: overtime, expediters, everything
options.feedback: That’s what Jons told Burnside over lunch.

options.text: No: it was an ordinary few weeks
options.feedback: Right.

posts.reveal: No extra effort at all. Just the new way of running the plant. ‘Shhh,’ whispers Jons. ‘Don’t let Burnside know.’ Burnside wants a long-term contract: 10,000 Model 12s a year. And Jons owes Alex a pair of shoes.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.take: Reliable, short lead times turned the plant into marketing’s best argument.
posts.label: The turnaround
posts.head: On-time delivery is a sales weapon.
posts.sub: Jons is planning a campaign for everything Bearington makes: the one plant in the division that ships quality on time. Two workers watch Burnside go by. ‘Guess we must’ve done something right.’

posts.label: Forest Grove · the night before the review
posts.text: Julie says she finally understands why she hasn’t wanted to come home: apart, they’ve spent more time together than they did under one roof. Flowers. Walks. Attention. She wants more of him, not less. They promise to talk every evening again, the way they used to, and to see things from each other’s side.

‘So… you want to get married?’ ‘I’ll try anything twice.’ Vegas, tomorrow night. But first, the plant review at ten. Alex walks in to find Peach’s chair empty, and Hilton Smyth at the head of the table.

chapters.title: Gold Mine
chapters.hook: Peach’s chair is empty and Hilton Smyth is the judge. By lunch, Alex has a job he never asked for.
recap: At the review, Smyth insists rising product costs mean falling profits.
Peach keeps the plant open and makes Alex head of the division.
Jonah won’t come to help. First, Alex must work out what a manager needs to learn.

posts.head: Peach’s chair is empty. Hilton Smyth is running the review.
posts.sub: By lunchtime, Alex walks out with the biggest surprise of his career.

posts.t: Is the goal to reduce costs?
posts.label: 15th floor · conference room

msgs.text: I’d particularly like to know why you aren’t following proper procedures for batch quantities.
First a question. Is the goal of this division to reduce costs?
Of course it is.
No. The goal is to make money. Agreed?
Whatever our costs look like by the standard measurements, my plant has never been in a better position to make money.

posts.label: An hour and a half later
left: A busy worker is a productive worker
An hour saved anywhere is saved
right: An hour saved at a non-bottleneck is a mirage
posts.text: Smyth isn’t moved. Costs per product went up, so profits must go down. That is what his report to Peach will say.

posts.label: Peach’s office
posts.text: Alex doesn’t take the elevator. He walks to Peach’s office. ‘Go right in,’ says his secretary. ‘He’s waiting for you.’ Peach calls in Smyth, the division controller and Johnny Jons. Smyth wants Alex called to order. The controller points out the plant turned losses into profits and released cash. Jons says it’s the only plant that delivers miracles. ‘Miracles exist only in fairy tales,’ sniffs Smyth.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: Rising product costs on one side. Profits, cash and delighted customers on the other. What does Peach decide?

options.text: Close it. The costs are rising.
options.feedback: Smyth would like that.

options.text: Keep it open, under Smyth’s supervision
options.feedback: Not quite.

options.text: Something nobody in the room expects
options.feedback: Right.

posts.reveal: ‘Do you think we’re such bad managers that we’d close a gold mine?’ Then the real news: Peach, the controller and Jons are moving up to run the group. Their choice to take over the division: Alex Rogo.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

msgs.text: All this time I was trying to save one plant. Now I’ll have three. Can’t you come and help?
As your responsibility grows, you should rely more on yourself. My coming now would increase the dependency.
Then teach me how to manage. A plant, a division, any organization.
Good. First assignment: work out what techniques effective management needs. Call me when you know.

posts.label: A restaurant · that evening
posts.text: Alex tries to give Jonah all the credit. Julie won’t have it: nobody handed him answers, he sweated for them. Then she asks the real question. If the answers are just common sense, why couldn’t they see them alone? Alex’s best guess: common sense gets buried under common practice. Jonah’s questions peel the practice away.

posts.head: They made more money than the books said.
posts.text: Lou finds a bigger distortion. Inventory is counted as an asset at full production cost, so draining half the work-in-process showed up as a loss. Real net profit: over 20% in each of the last three months. He told the division controller, not Alex. That’s why the controller was so supportive.

posts.label: Alex’s office · the next day

items.text: Lou: joins the division to build measurements that make sense
Bob: stays as plant manager, to engineer sales like Burnside’s
Stacey: production manager, watching the buffers for holes
Ralph: systems that answer the questions people actually ask

posts.text: Each of them knows exactly what they want to build. Alex has only Jonah’s question.

Two months left. Every afternoon, Alex asks his team to help him answer Jonah’s question. He begins innocently: what should a new division manager do first? Their answer covers a whiteboard in colored circles and leads absolutely nowhere.

chapters.title: Your Own Jonah
chapters.hook: How do you find the weakest link in an entire company? They write down what they did, and discover what they forgot.
recap: Five steps: identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, and never let inertia become the constraint.
Spare capacity is protection, and also an opportunity to sell.
A manager must answer three questions: what to change, what to change to, how to cause the change.

posts.head: How do you find the weakest link in a whole company?
posts.sub: The team writes down what they actually did. Then they discover what they forgot.

posts.label: The conference room
posts.text: Collect all the facts first, the team suggests. Alex fills the whiteboard with colored circles, stars and squares. Sort them by color? By size? By shape? ‘I’d rather throw darts,’ says Bob. Ralph tells the story of Mendeleev, who found the order hidden in the chemical elements and predicted ones nobody had found. Sorting by any convenient label just produces thick reports.

posts.label: Lou’s discovery
posts.h: From the cost world to the throughput world
left: Every link matters, like a chain’s weight
right: The weakest link sets the strength
posts.text: Their own numbers prove it: throughput and inventory moved by tens of percent, operating expense by less than 2%.

posts.take: Identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat, and beware inertia.
posts.label: Written on the whiteboard
posts.h: The process they had been following

items.text: 3. SUBORDINATE everything else to that decision
5. If a constraint breaks, go back to step 1. Don’t let INERTIA become the constraint.

posts.text: Furnaces and the NCX-10; no idle breaks; red tags and timed releases; the Zmegma. Each step matches something they did.

posts.head: Their own fixes had become the constraint.
posts.text: With work now released at the right pace, the red tags only made some machines delay green parts. And when bottleneck load dropped, Stacey kept the bottlenecks busy building stock nobody had ordered: a fifth of their load. Their newest habits had gone stale in under a month.

posts.label: You decide
posts.q: A French buyer offers $701 for the Model 12. The list price is $992; materials cost $334. Jons says it’s below cost: forget it. You have spare capacity. Take it?

options.text: No. It’s below product cost.
options.feedback: That’s Jons’ answer.

options.text: Yes. It’s far above material cost.
options.feedback: That’s Alex’s answer.

posts.reveal: With spare capacity, the only extra cost is materials and freight, so each unit adds hundreds of dollars to profit. To avoid a price war, Alex competes on speed instead: delivery in three weeks, where Europe waits eight to twelve. Seven-figure profit.
posts.hint: Pick one to see what actually happened.

posts.label: Two weeks later
posts.text: Twelve work centers on overtime. Orders starting to slip. The bottlenecks starve, then get flooded. The cause: after any breakdown, upstream machines must feed the bottleneck and rebuild its buffer at the same time. The new orders ate the spare capacity that made that possible. Bob takes charge: bigger buffers, weekend work, four-week quotes. The baton has passed.

posts.take: Buffers and spare capacity trade off; without either, the bottleneck starves.
posts.label: The lesson
posts.head: Non-bottlenecks need spare capacity.
posts.sub: Less buffer in front of a bottleneck needs more spare capacity upstream, and the reverse. A plant with no idle capacity anywhere can’t even keep its bottleneck busy.

msgs.text: In the division the constraints aren’t machines. They’re policies. Even in our plant, they were.
Then we need a way to find the core problem. And then what to replace it with.
And how to make the change happen. What to change, what to change to, how to cause the change.
We should and can be our own Jonahs.
Alex, I’m proud to work for you.

posts.text: Alex finally knows what to ask Jonah to teach him: not answers, but the thinking processes to find the core problem, design a solution that works, and bring people along. The plant is saved. The real lesson is the one he’ll keep using.
